claims.text: The initial material is a MoNbTaW-based refractory high-entropy alloy produced by conventional powder metallurgy without added nano-oxides.
Y2O3 nano-oxides will be added during mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering.
Tuning the milling and spark-plasma-sintering parameters can produce a homogeneous nano-oxide dispersion in the alloy.
The intervention will create stable, uniformly distributed nano-oxide particles in the high-entropy-alloy matrix.
The dispersed nano-oxides will impede dislocation motion through Orowan strengthening.
The nano-oxides will act as sinks that trap irradiation-induced point defects.
Defect trapping by the nano-oxides will mitigate the nucleation and growth of helium bubbles.
Nano-oxide addition will not compromise the alloy's high-temperature phase stability.
Relative to an oxide-free MoNbTaW-based control, the nano-oxide-containing alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to an oxide-free MoNbTaW-based control, the nano-oxide-containing alloy will have greater creep resistance.
The nano-oxide-containing alloy will maintain high-temperature stability at temperatures up to 900 °C.
The nano-oxide-containing alloy will resist irradiation-induced defect accumulation under approximately 200 keV helium irradiation at temperatures up to 900 °C.
Approximately 200 keV helium-ion irradiation can mimic relevant reactor irradiation conditions.
The beneficial effects require a uniform oxide dispersion without significant agglomeration.
Oxide agglomeration could offset the expected mechanical and irradiation-resistance benefits.
The expected performance improvements may not persist above 900 °C.
The expected performance improvements may not persist under irradiation conditions more severe than the simulated parameters.
